title: Reported speech
tagline: Telling someone what was said, one step back in time, person and place.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Listening Part 2/4 — following who said what
Speaking Part 1 — reporting what a friend or family member told you
why: The moment you repeat someone's words later, in a different place, the sentence has to move with you: tenses shift back, pronouns change, and tomorrow stops meaning anything. B2 First tests this constantly in Part 4, and getting the word order wrong in a reported question is one of the most common mistakes at this level.

diagrams.title: Direct speech to reported speech

before.text: Sofia said, "I finished the project yesterday."

after.text: Sofia said (that) she had finished the project the day before.

steps: Drop the quotation marks and add that (optional) after the reporting verb.
Move the verb one step back: finished → had finished.
Change the pronoun (I → she) and the time expression (yesterday → the day before).

diagrams.title: Time and place words move too
Reported questions: statement word order
diagrams.caption: No question mark, no auxiliary do/does/did, and the word order of a normal statement.

head: Direct speech
Reported speech
Example
rows: "I play chess." → He said he played chess.
"I'm studying." → She said she was studying.
"I've finished." → He said he had finished.
"I saw the match." → She said she had seen the match.
"I'll call you." → He said he would call me.
"I can help." → She said she could help.
"Do you agree?" → He asked if I agreed.
"Close the door." → She told him to close the door.

use.point: Reporting statements: the verb moves one step back, and so do pronouns, times and places

examples.text: Mateo said (that) he had missed the bus that morning.
Nadia told us (that) she was working on the essay then.
examples.note: now became then in reported speech

examples.text: Liam said he would meet us the next day.
examples.note: will → would; tomorrow → the next day

use.point: Reporting questions: yes/no questions with if/whether, wh-questions with the question word, both in statement order

examples.text: Miss Vega asked whether the group had finished the reading.
examples.note: yes/no question → whether + statement order, no auxiliary

examples.text: Sofia asked me if I wanted to join the debate club.
examples.note: if works exactly like whether here

examples.text: He asked her what time the rehearsal started.
examples.note: wh-question → wh-word + statement order, no question mark

use.point: Reporting commands and requests with tell/ask + object + to-infinitive

examples.text: The coach told the players to warm up before the match.
Nadia asked Liam not to slam the door during the test.

use.point: When the tense does not change: general truths, and modals with no past form

examples.text: Miss Vega said the Amazon rainforest covers a huge part of Peru.
examples.note: a fact that's still true → tense can stay the same

examples.text: Sofia said she should revise more before the exam.
examples.note: should, could, might, would, ought to don't backshift further

watch_out.wrong: She asked me did I like the film.
watch_out.right: She asked me if I liked the film.
watch_out.why: A reported question keeps statement word order — no inverted auxiliary.

watch_out.wrong: He asked me what did I want for lunch.
watch_out.right: He asked me what I wanted for lunch.
watch_out.why: No did and no inversion in a reported wh-question — it follows normal sentence order.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher told us to not run in the corridor.
watch_out.right: The teacher told us not to run in the corridor.
watch_out.why: The negative goes before to, not between to and the verb.

watch_out.wrong: She said she will see me tomorrow.
watch_out.right: She said she would see me the next day.
watch_out.why: Both the modal and the time expression need to shift when you report it later.

watch_out.wrong: He asked if did she finish her homework?
watch_out.right: He asked if she had finished her homework.
watch_out.why: A reported question is not a question anymore — no question mark, no auxiliary before the subject.

watch_out.wrong: Liam told that he was tired.
watch_out.why: Tell needs an object (tell someone); use said when there's no object stated.

dialogue.title: Catching up after being away
dialogue.context: Mateo was away sick for two days. Sofia, Liam and Nadia fill him in on what happened at school in Lima.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: So what did I miss? Start with the science project.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Miss Vega said the deadline had been moved to next Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: And she asked if everyone had chosen a topic yet — you'll need to tell her yours.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Right. Anything about the trip to Cusco?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes, she told us to bring our forms back by Friday, no exceptions.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Oh, and Liam's coach asked him whether he could play in Saturday's match.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I told him I would confirm after checking with my parents.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: What about the assembly on Tuesday? I heard there was an announcement.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: The head teacher said the new library would open in October.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: That's great news. Thanks for catching me up — I told my mum I'd find out everything today.

items.sentence: Sofia said she ___ tired after the match.
items.why: present simple in direct speech → past simple in reported speech

items.sentence: He asked me ___ I had finished the report.
Nadia asked Liam what time the film ___.
items.why: reported wh-question keeps statement word order, no auxiliary

items.sentence: The coach told the team ___ warm up properly.
Mateo said he ___ call us later that evening.
items.why: will backshifts to would in reported speech

items.sentence: Miss Vega told us the Andes ___ through several South American countries — that's just a fact.
items.why: a general truth doesn't need to backshift

practice.instructions: Rewrite each part in reported speech, using the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: "I'm studying for the exam," Nadia said. → Nadia said she ___ (study) for the exam.
"Have you seen my notebook?" Liam asked. → Liam asked if I ___ (see) his notebook.
"Don't touch my laptop," Sofia said. → Sofia told me ___ (not/touch) her laptop.
"We will arrive tomorrow," they said. → They said they ___ (arrive) the next day.
"Where do you live?" the interviewer asked. → The interviewer asked me where I ___ (live).
"I can't come to the party," Mateo said. → Mateo said he ___ (not/can) come to the party.
"I saw the results yesterday," Sofia said. → Sofia said she ___ (see) the results the day before.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: "I finished the essay this morning," Nadia said.
"Will you help me with the poster?" Liam asked Sofia.
"Don't be late for practice," the coach told the team.
"Where did you buy that jacket?" Nadia asked Mateo.
"I can't attend the meeting tomorrow," Sofia said.

summary: Reporting a statement usually moves the verb one tense back: am/is/are → was/were, will → would, have done → had done.
Pronouns, times and places shift too: I → he/she, tomorrow → the next day, here → there.
Reported questions never keep question word order: no do/does/did, no inversion, no question mark.
Commands and requests become tell/ask + object + (not) to-infinitive.
A fact that's still true, or a modal like would, could, should, doesn't need to move any further back.
